Badgers
BAJ-erz
n. pl.
English badger, a burrowing animal; Webster 1828 defines the animal. In the Authorized Version the word survives only in the fixed phrase badgers' skins, the outermost covering of the tabernacle and of its vessels in transit. The Hebrew tachash is disputed; the KJV translators chose an English animal of tough, weatherproof hide.

Biblical Definition

Badgers' skins are the outside of the house of God. In the list of materials for the tabernacle they come third, after gold and blue: And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood (Exodus 25:5). Over the fine twined linen, over the goats' hair, over the red-dyed rams' skins, God commands one more layer: a covering above of badgers' skins (Exodus 26:14). That is what Israel saw from the camp. The glory was inside; the outside was a tough, plain hide that turned the weather. When the ark and the vessels travelled, the same covering went with them: the Kohathites shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins (Numbers 4:6), and the golden altar likewise (Numbers 4:11). The one figurative use turns it into grace: the LORD says of Jerusalem, I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin (Ezekiel 16:10) — the sanctuary's own weatherproof leather made into shoes for a foundling bride. Isaiah's no form nor comeliness is the same shape of truth: the outside of what God builds is often the least impressive thing about it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BADGER as a quadruped of the genus Ursus, a burrowing animal, and notes the use of its skin for tough leather. The KJV uses the plural only of the outermost tabernacle covering, translating a Hebrew word whose animal is disputed but whose function — a durable weatherproof hide — is not.

expand to see more

BADGER, n. — A quadruped of the genus Ursus, a burrowing animal of nocturnal habits; the hide is thick and tough and has been used for leather.

The Hebrew tachash has been rendered badger, seal, porpoise, dolphin, and dugong by different hands; the KJV chose an English animal known for hide durable enough to shed rain.

The exegetical point does not turn on zoology. Whatever the creature, the layer is the outermost, the toughest, and the plainest — that is what the text requires of it in every occurrence.

Key Scripture

Exodus 25:5 — "And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood,"

Exodus 26:14 — "And thou shalt make a covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers' skins."

Numbers 4:6 — "And shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins, and shall spread over it a cloth wholly of blue, and shall put in the staves thereof."

Numbers 4:11 — "And upon the golden altar they shall spread a cloth of blue, and cover it with a covering of badgers' skins, and shall put to the staves thereof:"

Ezekiel 16:10 — "I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is the opposite of redefinition: a church that reverses the tabernacle’s order, spending on the outside what God spent on the inside, and judging spiritual worth by what shows from the camp.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The scholarly argument over which animal tachash names is real but harmless; every candidate yields the same tough outer hide. The genuine problem is that the tabernacle’s order of value has been inverted in practice. God put gold and cherubim and fine twined linen where only priests would see them, and put plain leather where the whole nation would look.

The principle to recover is that God builds from the inside out. Isaiah says of the Servant that he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him (Isaiah 53:2) — badgers' skins over the glory. Paul says the same of the ministry: we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us (2 Corinthians 4:7). A congregation that measures itself by its frontage has read the tabernacle backwards. And Ezekiel 16:10 keeps the tenderness in view: the same durable hide God used to shelter His house He used to shoe a bride He had found abandoned in a field.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is tachash, an animal or hide whose identity is disputed, standing always in the phrase 'oroth techashim, skins of tachash. The related noun for skin is 'or, the same word used of the coats God made for Adam and Eve.

expand to see more

Hebrew tachash (H8476) — the animal or hide of the outermost tabernacle covering (Exodus 25:5; 26:14; Numbers 4:6); rendered badgers by the KJV.

Hebrew 'or (H5785) — skin, hide; the same noun in coats of skins for Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:21), where a covering also costs a life.

The Septuagint renders the phrase with a word for hyacinth-coloured skins, showing the animal was already uncertain before the Christian era.

The covering order runs inward to outward: fine twined linen with cherubim, goats' hair, rams' skins dyed red, badgers' skins (Exodus 26:1-14).

Ezekiel 16:10 is the only non-tabernacle occurrence, and it transfers the sanctuary material to the clothing of a rescued bride.

Usage

"A covering above of badgers' skins (Exodus 26:14) — the outermost of four layers; the plainest thing is what the camp sees."

"The covering of badgers' skins (Numbers 4:6) — the holy things travel wrapped in the same weatherproof hide."

"Shod thee with badgers' skin (Ezekiel 16:10) — sanctuary leather made into shoes for a foundling; grace in the vocabulary of the tabernacle."
